title: Πρόκλησις καὶ ᾠδή
titleEn: The Challenge and the Song of Ares and Aphrodite — Odyssey 8.195–291
part: The Challenge and the Song of Ares and Aphrodite (8.195–291)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Athena, still in the shape of a man, tells Odysseus that his cast is far the longest, and he, glad of a friend, answers the Phaeacian youths who taunted him. He challenges any of them to box, wrestle or run, sparing only Laodamas, his host, and boasts of his bow and his spear, though he fears for his legs after the sea. Alcinous smooths the quarrel over, praises what the Phaeacians do well, ships, running, dance and song, and calls for the lyre. The ground is cleared, young dancers take their places, and Demodocus begins to sing of the secret love of Ares and Aphrodite: the Sun told Hephaestus, who forged bonds too fine to see, spread them round his bed, and set out for Lemnos. Ares saw him go, came to the house and took Aphrodite by the hand.

sentences.t:
καί κ’ ἀλαός τοι, ξεῖνε, διακρίνειε τὸ σῆμα
ἀμφαφόων, ἐπεὶ οὔ τι μεμιγμένον ἐστὶν ὁμίλῳ,
ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρῶτον.
sentences.tr:
kai k’ alaos toi, xeine, diakrineie to sēma
amphaphoōn, epei ou ti memigmenon estin homilōi,
alla poly prōton.
sentences.l:
“And even a blind man, for you, stranger, would tell the mark apart,
feeling it about, since it is not at all mixed with the throng,
but far the first.
sentences.i: “Even a blind man, stranger, could tell your mark apart by groping for it, since it is not at all mixed in with the throng, but is far the first.
sentences.n: This opens Athena's speech; at the end of the previous part she stood beside Odysseus in the likeness of a man. καί … κε with the optative διακρίνειε is 'even … would tell apart': κε(ν) is the Attic ἄν, and διακρίνω 'separate, distinguish'. ἀλαός is 'blind', here 'a blind man'; τοι is the pronoun 'to you, for you'; ἀμφαφόων is the uncontracted participle of ἀμφαφάω 'feel about, handle' (Attic ἀμφαφῶν). μεμιγμένον is the perfect passive participle of μίγνυμι 'mix', and ὁμίλῳ, the dative of ὅμιλος 'throng', is the crowd, taken here as the other marks. πολύ before πρῶτον is 'by far'. The stop after πρῶτον falls in the middle of line 197.

sentences.t: σὺ δὲ θάρσει τόνδε γ’ ἄεθλον·
sentences.tr: sy de tharsei tonde g’ aethlon·
sentences.l: and you, take heart, in this contest at least;
sentences.i: But take heart, in this contest at least;
sentences.n: σὺ δέ 'and you' turns to the stranger. θάρσει is the imperative of θαρσέω 'be of good courage'. τόνδε … ἄεθλον is an accusative of respect, 'as regards this contest', and γε limits it: 'in this one, at least'. ἄεθλον is the singular of the word for 'contest' that returns through the speeches of this part (ἀέθλων at 210, ἄεθλοι at 214).

sentences.t: οὔ τις Φαιήκων τόδε γ’ ἵξεται, οὐδ’ ὑπερήσει.
sentences.tr: ou tis Phaiēkōn tode g’ hixetai, oud’ hyperēsei.
sentences.l: not one of the Phaeacians will reach this, nor throw beyond it.”
sentences.i: No Phaeacian will reach this, or throw beyond it.”
sentences.n: οὔ τις 'no one'; ἵξεται is the future of ἱκνέομαι 'arrive at, reach', with τόδε as its object. ὑπερήσει is the future of ὑπερίημι 'throw beyond', the same verb as ἥσειν 'to hurl' at 203 (ἵημι). Two plain futures state it flatly, with no ἄν. The γε after τόδε repeats the emphasis of τόνδε γ’ in the line before and is not translated separately. The closing quotation mark ends Athena's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, γήθησεν δὲ πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
χαίρων, οὕνεχ’ ἑταῖρον ἐνηέα λεῦσσ’ ἐν ἀγῶνι.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, gēthēsen de polytlas dios Odysseus,
chairōn, hounech’ hetairon enēea leuss’ en agōni.
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and rejoiced much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
being glad that a kindly companion he saw in the gathering.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus rejoiced, glad to see a kindly companion in the gathering.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο 'so she spoke' closes Athena's speech: φάτο is ἔφατο without the augment, and the speaker is the goddess, still in a man's shape. γήθησεν is the aorist of γηθέω 'rejoice'. πολύτλας 'much-enduring' and δῖος 'heavenly' are Odysseus's standing epithets and are translated the same way each time. In the second line οὕνεχ’ is οὕνεκα 'because'; ἑταῖρον ἐνηέα 'a kindly companion' (ἐνηής 'kindly, gentle') is the object of λεῦσσ’, the elided imperfect of λεύσσω 'look at, see'; Odysseus does not know that the companion is Athena. ἐν ἀγῶνι is 'in the gathering': ἀγών is the gathering of people for the games and the ground where they meet, and is kept distinct from ἄεθλον 'contest'.

sentences.t: καὶ τότε κουφότερον μετεφώνεε Φαιήκεσσιν·
sentences.tr: kai tote kouphoteron metephōnee Phaiēkessin·
sentences.l: And then more lightly he spoke among the Phaeacians:
sentences.i: And then, more lightly, he spoke among the Phaeacians:
sentences.n: καὶ τότε 'and then'. κουφότερον is the comparative adverb of κοῦφος 'light', 'more lightly', of his manner after the joy just described. μετεφώνεε is the uncontracted imperfect of μεταφωνέω 'speak among' (Attic μετεφώνει), the same 'speak among' as μετέειπε; Φαιήκεσσιν is the dative plural 'the Phaeacians'. The stop · announces the speech.

sentences.t: τοῦτον νῦν ἀφίκεσθε, νέοι.
sentences.tr: touton nyn aphikesthe, neoi.
sentences.l: “This one now reach, young men.
sentences.i: “Now reach this one, young men.
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks now to the Phaeacian youths. ἀφίκεσθε is the aorist imperative of ἀφικνέομαι 'arrive at, reach', with τοῦτον as its object; τοῦτον is masculine and the Greek does not say what it stands for (δίσκος and λίθος, the discus and the stone, are both masculine), so 'this one' is left as it stands. νέοι is 'young men'. The stop after νέοι falls in the middle of line 202.

sentences.t:
τάχα δ’ ὕστερον ἄλλον
ἥσειν ἢ τοσσοῦτον ὀίομαι ἢ ἔτι μᾶσσον.
sentences.tr:
tacha d’ hysteron allon
hēsein ē tossouton oiomai ē eti masson.
sentences.l:
and soon, afterwards, another
to hurl, either as far, I think, or still farther.
sentences.i: Soon afterwards I think I shall hurl another, either as far or farther still.
sentences.n: τάχα is 'soon', ὕστερον 'afterwards', and ἄλλον 'another', a second one of the same kind. ἥσειν is the future infinitive of ἵημι 'hurl' after ὀίομαι 'I think' (the subject of the infinitive, ἐμέ, is left out because it is also the subject of ὀίομαι: 'that I shall hurl'). τοσσοῦτον is τοσοῦτον 'so far, so much', with the doubled σ Homer often writes, and μᾶσσον is the neuter comparative of μακρός 'long', 'farther'; ἢ … ἢ … is 'either … or …'.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄλλων ὅτινα κραδίη θυμός τε κελεύει,
δεῦρ’ ἄγε πειρηθήτω, ἐπεί μ’ ἐχολώσατε λίην,
ἢ πὺξ ἠὲ πάλῃ ἢ καὶ ποσίν, οὔ τι μεγαίρω,
πάντων Φαιήκων, πλήν γ’ αὐτοῦ Λαοδάμαντος.
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ allōn hotina kradiē thymos te keleuei,
deur’ age peirēthētō, epei m’ echolōsate liēn,
ē pyx ēe palēi ē kai posin, ou ti megairō,
pantōn Phaiēkōn, plēn g’ autou Laodamantos.
sentences.l:
But of the others, whomever heart and spirit bid,
come here, let him try, since you angered me exceedingly,
either boxing or wrestling or even with feet, I do not begrudge it,
of all the Phaeacians, except Laodamas himself.
sentences.i: Of the rest, whoever his heart and spirit urge, let him come here and make trial, since you have angered me so greatly, at boxing or wrestling or even running; I begrudge it to none of the Phaeacians, except Laodamas himself.
sentences.n: τῶν δ’ ἄλλων 'and of the others' is a partitive genitive, 'whoever of the rest'. ὅτινα is ὅντινα 'whomever'; κελεύει 'bids'; κραδίη 'heart' and θυμός 'spirit' are kept apart because they stand together. πειρηθήτω is the third-person imperative of πειράω 'make trial'; the object is left unsaid. ἐχολώσατε 'you angered' is aorist. ἢ … ἠέ … ἢ is 'either … or … or'; πύξ 'with the fist' (boxing), πάλῃ 'in wrestling', ποσίν 'with the feet' (running). οὔ τι μεγαίρω 'I do not begrudge it at all'; μεγαίρω 'begrudge, refuse'. πάντων Φαιήκων 'of all the Phaeacians' is a genitive of the persons not begrudged, with 'to any' understood, as the English takes it. πλήν γε 'except', with αὐτοῦ 'himself', names the one person left out; the next line says why.

sentences.t: ξεῖνος γάρ μοι ὅδ’ ἐστί·
sentences.tr: xeinos gar moi hod’ esti·
sentences.l: For to me this one is a guest-friend;
sentences.i: For he is my guest-friend;
sentences.n: ξεῖνος is not 'stranger' here but 'guest-friend', someone joined to you by the give and take of hospitality; the whole passage turns on it. μοι is 'to me' and ὅδ’ 'this one here' points at Laodamas, whom Odysseus has just excepted. γάρ 'for' explains that exception.

sentences.t: τίς ἂν φιλέοντι μάχοιτο;
sentences.tr: tis an phileonti machoito;
sentences.l: who would fight with one who befriends him?
sentences.i: who would fight with a man who treats him kindly?
sentences.n: τίς ἂν … μάχοιτο; is a potential question, 'who would fight?', and it expects the answer 'no one'. φιλέοντι is the dative participle of φιλέω 'love, treat as a friend', and μάχομαι takes the dative 'fight with'. The stop ; falls in the middle of line 208.

sentences.t:
ἄφρων δὴ κεῖνός γε καὶ οὐτιδανὸς πέλει ἀνήρ,
ὅς τις ξεινοδόκῳ ἔριδα προφέρηται ἀέθλων
δήμῳ ἐν ἀλλοδαπῷ·
sentences.tr:
aphrōn dē keinos ge kai outidanos pelei anēr,
hos tis xeinodokōi erida propherētai aethlōn
dēmōi en allodapōi·
sentences.i: Senseless and worthless indeed is the man who, in a foreign land, brings strife against his host over contests;
sentences.n: ἄφρων 'senseless' and οὐτιδανός 'worthless, a nobody' (built on οὔτις 'no one', by the usual account) are two predicates of κεῖνος … ἀνήρ 'that man' (κεῖνος is the Ionic form of ἐκεῖνος); πέλει is 'is'. ὅς τις 'whoever' begins a general relative clause with the subjunctive προφέρηται (προφέρω 'bring forward, offer'), which needs no ἄν or κε in Homer. ξεινοδόκῳ 'to his host' (one who receives a ξεῖνος), ἔριδα 'strife', ἀέθλων 'of contests', so 'strife over contests'. δήμῳ ἐν ἀλλοδαπῷ: δῆμος here is 'district, land', not 'the people', and ἀλλοδαπός is 'of another land'. The stop · after ἀλλοδαπῷ is in the middle of line 211.

sentences.t: ἕο δ’ αὐτοῦ πάντα κολούει.
sentences.tr: heo d’ autou panta kolouei.
sentences.l: and of his own everything he cuts short.
sentences.i: and he cuts short everything that is his own.
sentences.n: ἕο is the epic genitive of the reflexive pronoun ἕ, 'of himself' (Attic οὗ), and αὐτοῦ strengthens it, 'of his very self'; with πάντα it gives 'everything of his own'. κολούει is 'cuts short, curtails, mars'. The clause is compressed and its exact sense is not certain: it says that the man who picks such a quarrel damages all that is his own, presumably his standing and his prospects, but the Greek does not say which.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄλλων οὔ πέρ τιν’ ἀναίνομαι οὐδ’ ἀθερίζω,
ἀλλ’ ἐθέλω ἴδμεν καὶ πειρηθήμεναι ἄντην.
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ allōn ou per tin’ anainomai oud’ atherizō,
all’ ethelō idmen kai peirēthēmenai antēn.
sentences.l:
But of the others I refuse none nor make light of any,
but I wish to know and to make trial face to face.
sentences.i: As for the rest, I turn none of them away and think little of none, but I want to know, and to make trial face to face.
sentences.n: οὔ πέρ τιν’ … οὐδ’ is 'not any … nor', with emphatic πέρ. ἀναίνομαι is 'refuse, decline', ἀθερίζω 'slight, treat lightly'. ἴδμεν is the infinitive of οἶδα 'know' (Attic εἰδέναι), and πειρηθήμεναι the aorist infinitive of πειράω 'make trial' with the ending -μεναι (Attic πειραθῆναι); it is passive in form but active in sense, as is πειρηθήτω at 205. ἄντην is 'face to face, openly'.

sentences.t: πάντα γὰρ οὐ κακός εἰμι, μετ’ ἀνδράσιν ὅσσοι ἄεθλοι·
sentences.tr: panta gar ou kakos eimi, met’ andrasin hossoi aethloi·
sentences.l: for in everything I am not bad, among men, as many as are contests;
sentences.i: for I am not poor at any of them, of all the contests there are among men;
sentences.n: πάντα is an accusative of respect, 'in all things'. οὐ κακός 'not bad' says 'good' by denying the opposite. μετ’ ἀνδράσιν 'among men'; ὅσσοι ἄεθλοι 'as many contests as there are', with the doubled σ of ὅσσοι.

sentences.t: εὖ μὲν τόξον οἶδα ἐύξοον ἀμφαφάασθαι·
sentences.tr: eu men toxon oida eyxoon amphaphaasthai·
sentences.l: well indeed the bow, the well-polished, I know how to handle;
sentences.i: I know well how to handle a well-polished bow;
sentences.n: εὖ μέν 'well indeed', the μέν pointing on to the next boast. οἶδα with an infinitive is 'know how to'. ἀμφαφάασθαι is the uncontracted infinitive (Attic ἀμφαφᾶσθαι) of ἀμφαφάομαι 'handle, feel over', the verb behind ἀμφαφόων at 196. ἐύξοον 'well-polished' (ἐύξοος, 'well smoothed') agrees with τόξον 'bow'.

sentences.t:
πρῶτός κ’ ἄνδρα βάλοιμι ὀιστεύσας ἐν ὁμίλῳ
ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων, εἰ καὶ μάλα πολλοὶ ἑταῖροι
ἄγχι παρασταῖεν καὶ τοξαζοίατο φωτῶν.
sentences.tr:
prōtos k’ andra baloimi oisteusas en homilōi
andrōn dysmeneōn, ei kai mala polloi hetairoi
anchi parastaien kai toxazoiato phōtōn.
sentences.l:
First I would strike a man, having shot an arrow, in the throng
of hostile men, even if very many companions
stood close by and shot at men.
sentences.i: I would be the first to strike a man with an arrow in a throng of hostile men, even if very many companions stood close by and shot at men.
sentences.n: κε with the optative βάλοιμι is 'I would hit'; πρῶτος 'first' says he would be first; ὀιστεύσας is the aorist participle of ὀιστεύω 'shoot an arrow' (ὀιστός 'arrow'). ἐν ὁμίλῳ ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων 'in the throng of hostile men' (δυσμενής 'ill-disposed, hostile'). εἰ καὶ μάλα 'even if very much' takes two optatives, παρασταῖεν (aorist of παρίστημι, with the ending -αῖεν) and τοξαζοίατο (τοξάζομαι 'shoot with the bow', third plural in -οίατο). ἑταῖροι 'companions' are, on the reading taken here, his own, and φωτῶν is the genitive after τοξαζοίατο, 'shoot at men'; the Greek would also allow φωτῶν to go with ἑταῖροι.

sentences.t:
οἶος δή με Φιλοκτήτης ἀπεκαίνυτο τόξῳ
δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων, ὅτε τοξαζοίμεθ’ Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
oios dē me Philoktētēs apekainyto toxōi
dēmōi eni Trōōn, hote toxazoimeth’ Achaioi.
sentences.l:
Alone indeed Philoctetes used to outdo me with the bow
in the land of the Trojans, whenever we Achaeans shot with the bow.
sentences.i: Only Philoctetes used to outdo me with the bow, in the land of the Trojans, whenever we Achaeans shot.
sentences.n: οἶος 'alone, only' agrees with Φιλοκτήτης, the one archer Odysseus admits to be better than himself. ἀπεκαίνυτο is the imperfect of ἀποκαίνυμαι (καίνυμαι 'surpass'), 'used to outdo', with με 'me' as object and τόξῳ 'with the bow' as instrument. ὅτε τοξαζοίμεθ’ is the optative in a general clause, 'whenever we shot with the bow'. δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων is 'in the land of the Trojans': ἔνι is ἐνί 'in', placed after its noun, and δῆμος is 'land' as at 211.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄλλων ἐμέ φημι πολὺ προφερέστερον εἶναι,
ὅσσοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσιν ἐπὶ χθονὶ σῖτον ἔδοντες.
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ allōn eme phēmi poly propheresteron einai,
hossoi nyn brotoi eisin epi chthoni siton edontes.
sentences.l:
of the others I say that I am far better,
as many as are now mortals on the earth eating bread.
sentences.i: Of the rest I say that I am far better than all who are now mortals on the earth, eating bread.
sentences.n: φημι governs an accusative and infinitive, ἐμέ … εἶναι 'that I am'. προφερέστερον is the comparative of προφερής 'better, superior' (related to προφέρω 'bring forward, excel'), with πολύ 'by far'. ὅσσοι … βροτοί εἰσιν 'as many as are mortals'; σῖτον ἔδοντες 'eating bread' (σῖτος is grain, bread, food; ἔδοντες is the participle of ἔδω 'eat') describes mortals as the people who live on grain, as opposed to the gods.

sentences.t:
ἀνδράσι δὲ προτέροισιν ἐριζέμεν οὐκ ἐθελήσω,
οὔθ’ Ἡρακλῆι οὔτ’ Εὐρύτῳ Οἰχαλιῆι,
οἵ ῥα καὶ ἀθανάτοισιν ἐρίζεσκον περὶ τόξων.
sentences.tr:
andrasi de proteroisin erizemen ouk ethelēsō,
outh’ Hēraklēi out’ Eurytōi Oichaliēi,
hoi rha kai athanatoisin erizeskon peri toxōn.
sentences.l:
But with men of earlier days I will not consent to vie,
neither with Heracles nor with Eurytus of Oechalia,
who even with the immortals used to vie about bows.
sentences.i: But I will not agree to vie with men of earlier days, neither with Heracles nor with Eurytus of Oechalia, who used to vie even with the immortals over bows.
sentences.n: ἀνδράσι … προτέροισιν is a dative after ἐριζέμεν 'to vie with', with the epic infinitive ending -έμεν (Attic ἐρίζειν); προτέροισιν 'earlier', of men of an earlier generation, has the ending -οισιν. οὔθ’ … οὔτ’ 'neither … nor' brings in the two names. Εὐρύτῳ Οἰχαλιῆι is 'Eurytus of Oechalia' (Οἰχαλιεύς 'man of Oechalia', dative). οἵ ῥα 'who indeed'; ἐρίζεσκον has the iterative suffix -σκ-, 'used to vie, kept vying'; ἀθανάτοισιν 'the immortals' is a plain noun here, and περὶ τόξων 'about bows'.

sentences.t:
τῷ ῥα καὶ αἶψ’ ἔθανεν μέγας Εὔρυτος, οὐδ’ ἐπὶ γῆρας
ἵκετ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισι·
sentences.tr:
tōi rha kai aips’ ethanen megas Eurytos, oud’ epi gēras
hiket’ eni megaroisi·
sentences.l:
Therefore indeed and quickly died great Eurytus, nor to old age
came he in his halls;
sentences.i: And so great Eurytus died quickly, and did not come to old age in his halls;
sentences.n: τῷ is 'therefore, for that reason' (an old dative of the demonstrative); it points forward to the reason given at 227. τῷ ῥα καὶ αἶψ’ ἔθανεν is 'so it was that he died quickly': αἶψ’ is αἶψα 'quickly', and ἔθανεν is the aorist of θνῄσκω. ἵκετ’ is ἵκετο 'he reached', the unaugmented past tense of ἱκνέομαι; ἐπὶ γῆρας 'to old age'; ἐνὶ μεγάροισι 'in his halls', with ἐνί = ἐν and the dative ending -οισι. The stop · falls in the middle of line 227.

sentences.t:
χολωσάμενος γὰρ Ἀπόλλων
ἔκτανεν, οὕνεκά μιν προκαλίζετο τοξάζεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
cholōsamenos gar Apollōn
ektanen, houneka min prokalizeto toxazesthai.
sentences.l:
for having grown angry, Apollo
killed him, because him he was challenging to shoot with the bow.
sentences.i: for Apollo, angered, killed him, because he had challenged him to shoot with the bow.
sentences.n: γάρ 'for' gives the reason for the early death. χολωσάμενος is the aorist participle of χολόομαι 'be angered' (compare ἐχολώσατε at 205). ἔκτανεν is the aorist of κτείνω 'kill'; οὕνεκα 'because'. μιν 'him' is Apollo, the one challenged, and the object of ἔκτανεν, Eurytus, is left unstated. προκαλίζετο 'was challenging' is the imperfect of προκαλίζομαι, and τοξάζεσθαι 'to shoot with the bow' says what he was challenged to.

sentences.t: δουρὶ δ’ ἀκοντίζω ὅσον οὐκ ἄλλος τις ὀιστῷ.
sentences.tr: douri d’ akontizō hoson ouk allos tis oistōi.
sentences.l: and with a spear I throw as far as no other man with an arrow.
sentences.i: And I can throw a spear as far as no other man can shoot an arrow.
sentences.n: δουρί is δορί, the dative of δόρυ 'spear'; ἀκοντίζω 'throw a javelin'. ὅσον οὐκ ἄλλος τις ὀιστῷ leaves out its verb, 'as far as no one else [shoots] with an arrow': the boast is that his spear carries farther than any other man's arrow.

sentences.t:
οἴοισιν δείδοικα ποσὶν μή τίς με παρέλθῃ
Φαιήκων·
sentences.tr:
oioisin deidoika posin mē tis me parelthēi
Phaiēkōn·
sentences.l:
For my feet alone I fear lest any pass me
of the Phaeacians;
sentences.i: It is only for my feet that I fear, lest some Phaeacian outstrip me;
sentences.n: οἴοισιν … ποσίν is 'for my feet alone', οἶος 'alone' agreeing with ποσίν in the dative plural; the dative gives the respect in which he fears. δείδοικα is the perfect of δείδω 'fear', taken as a present, and μή with the subjunctive παρέλθῃ (παρέρχομαι 'go past, outstrip') is 'lest'. τίς … Φαιήκων 'any of the Phaeacians'. The stop · after Φαιήκων is in the middle of line 231.

sentences.t:
λίην γὰρ ἀεικελίως ἐδαμάσθην
κύμασιν ἐν πολλοῖς, ἐπεὶ οὐ κομιδὴ κατὰ νῆα
ἦεν ἐπηετανός·
sentences.tr:
liēn gar aeikeliōs edamasthēn
kymasin en pollois, epei ou komidē kata nēa
ēen epēetanos·
sentences.i: for I was shamefully overpowered by many waves, since there was no never-failing care on board the ship;
sentences.n: λίην is 'exceedingly'; ἀεικελίως 'in an unseemly way, shamefully' is the adverb of ἀεικέλιος. ἐδαμάσθην is the aorist passive of δαμάζω 'overpower, tame', 'I was overpowered'. κύμασιν ἐν πολλοῖς 'among many waves'. κομιδή is 'care, tending', which may include supplying a man with food; κατὰ νῆα 'on board the ship' (κατά with the accusative, 'along'). ἦεν is ἦν 'was', and ἐπηετανός, 'never-failing, abundant', is a word whose sense is only approximately known; it is the complement, so the clause says that steady care was not there. The stop · falls in the middle of line 233.

sentences.t: τῷ μοι φίλα γυῖα λέλυνται.
sentences.tr: tōi moi phila guia lelyntai.
sentences.l: therefore to me my dear limbs are loosened.”
sentences.i: and so my limbs are slack.”
sentences.n: τῷ 'therefore' again, now giving the result. φίλα γυῖα is 'my dear limbs': with a part of the body φίλος is the possessive 'my own', and γυῖα is 'limbs'. λέλυνται is the perfect passive of λύω 'loosen', 'have been loosened, are slack'. μοι 'to me' is the dative of the sufferer. The closing quotation mark ends Odysseus's speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes akēn egenonto siōpēi.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ 'so he spoke' is ἔφατο, elided (the τ becomes θ before the rough breathing of οἱ), a middle form of φημί. οἱ δ’ ἄρα 'and they then': οἱ is the article as a pronoun, 'they'. ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ is 'they became hushed in silence': ἀκήν is an adverb-like word 'quietly, hushed', σιωπῇ the dative of σιωπή 'silence', and ἐγένοντο the aorist of γίγνομαι.

sentences.t: Ἀλκίνοος δέ μιν οἶος ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.tr: Alkinoos de min oios ameibomenos proseeipen·
sentences.l: but Alcinous, him, alone, answering addressed:
sentences.i: Alcinous alone spoke to him in answer:
sentences.n: This is a reply-formula. οἶος 'alone' agrees with Ἀλκίνοος: he alone answered, none of the other Phaeacians. μιν is 'him', Odysseus. ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν 'answering, he addressed' is a participle and a finite verb (προσέειπεν, the aorist of προσεῖπον 'speak to'). His words follow.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἀχάριστα μεθ’ ἡμῖν ταῦτ’ ἀγορεύεις,
ἀλλ’ ἐθέλεις ἀρετὴν σὴν φαινέμεν, ἥ τοι ὀπηδεῖ,
sentences.tr:
xein’, epei ouk acharista meth’ hēmin taut’ agoreueis,
all’ etheleis aretēn sēn phainemen, hē toi opēdei,
sentences.l:
“Stranger, since not ungraciously among us these things you say,
but you wish your excellence to show, which attends you,
sentences.i: “Stranger, since what you say among us is not ungracious, but you wish to show the excellence that goes with you,
sentences.n: ἐπεί 'since' begins a long subordinate clause that runs to 240; the main clause comes only with ἀλλ’ ἄγε at 241. ξεῖν’ is ξεῖνε 'stranger'. οὐκ ἀχάριστα is a litotes, 'not ungracious, not without grace'. μεθ’ ἡμῖν 'among us'; ἀγορεύεις 'you speak'. ἀρετή is 'excellence': in Homer it is a man's prowess, his fitness for what he has to do, rather than moral virtue. ἥ τοι ὀπηδεῖ 'which attends you': ἥ is the relative, 'which', and ὀπηδέω 'follow, attend'. φαινέμεν is φαίνειν 'to show', the -έμεν ending again.

sentences.t:
χωόμενος ὅτι σ’ οὗτος ἀνὴρ ἐν ἀγῶνι παραστὰς
νείκεσεν, ὡς ἂν σὴν ἀρετὴν βροτὸς οὔ τις ὄνοιτο,
ὅς τις ἐπίσταιτο ᾗσι φρεσὶν ἄρτια βάζειν·
sentences.tr:
chōomenos hoti s’ houtos anēr en agōni parastas
neikesen, hōs an sēn aretēn brotos ou tis onoito,
hos tis epistaito hēisi phresin artia bazein·
sentences.i: angry because this man stood beside you in the gathering and reviled you, in a way that no mortal would find fault with your excellence, no man who knew in his own mind how to speak what is fitting;
sentences.n: χωόμενος 'being angered' (χώομαι) agrees with the σύ understood in ἐθέλεις. ὅτι 'because'; οὗτος ἀνήρ 'this man' is Euryalus, who is not named here; ἐν ἀγῶνι 'in the gathering'; παραστάς 'having stood beside' (aorist participle of παρίστημι); νείκεσεν 'reviled' (aorist of νεικέω). ὡς ἂν … ὄνοιτο is not simple: ὄνοιτο is the optative of ὄνομαι 'find fault with, disparage', and the sense taken here is that the abuse was of a kind that no mortal with any sense would count as a fault in your excellence. ὅς τις ἐπίσταιτο 'whoever knew how to' (optative of ἐπίσταμαι), ᾗσι φρεσίν 'in his own mind' (the possessive ὅς again, with the dative plural of φρήν), ἄρτια βάζειν 'to speak fitting things' (ἄρτιος 'fitting, sound').

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ἐμέθεν ξυνίει ἔπος, ὄφρα καὶ ἄλλῳ
εἴπῃς ἡρώων, ὅτε κεν σοῖς ἐν μεγάροισι
δαινύῃ παρὰ σῇ τ’ ἀλόχῳ καὶ σοῖσι τέκεσσιν,
sentences.tr:
all’ age nyn emethen xyniei epos, ophra kai allōi
eipēis hērōōn, hote ken sois en megaroisi
dainyēi para sēi t’ alochōi kai soisi tekessin,
sentences.l:
But come now, from me take in a word, so that to another of the heroes also
you may tell, whenever in your halls
you feast beside your wife and your children,
sentences.i: But come now, take in what I say, so that you may tell it to another of the heroes as well, whenever you feast in your halls beside your wife and children,
sentences.n: This is the main clause the ἐπεί-clause was waiting for. ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν 'but come now' introduces a command; ξυνίει is the imperative of συνίημι 'take in, understand', with ἐμέθεν 'from me' (an old genitive of ἐγώ) and ἔπος 'word'. ὄφρα … εἴπῃς 'so that you may tell' (aorist subjunctive), ἄλλῳ … ἡρώων 'another of the heroes' (ἥρως 'hero'; the genitive is partitive). ὅτε κεν … δαινύῃ 'whenever you feast' (δαίνυμαι, subjunctive). σοῖς ἐν μεγάροισι 'in your halls'; παρὰ σῇ ἀλόχῳ 'beside your wife' (ἄλοχος); σοῖσι τέκεσσιν 'your children', with the ending -εσσι.

sentences.t:
ἡμετέρης ἀρετῆς μεμνημένος, οἷα καὶ ἡμῖν
Ζεὺς ἐπὶ ἔργα τίθησι διαμπερὲς ἐξ ἔτι πατρῶν.
sentences.tr:
hēmeterēs aretēs memnēmenos, hoia kai hēmin
Zeus epi erga tithēsi diamperes ex eti patrōn.
sentences.l:
of our excellence being mindful, of what kind to us also
Zeus lays upon works, unceasingly, from our fathers' time.
sentences.i: remembering our excellence, such as Zeus lays on our works for us too, without a break since our fathers' day.
sentences.n: ἡμετέρης ἀρετῆς 'our excellence' is the genitive after μεμνημένος, the perfect participle of μιμνῄσκομαι 'remember, be mindful of'. οἷα 'of what kind, such as' begins a compressed clause: Zeus sets (τίθησι) something upon (ἐπί) works, and the sense taken here is that he crowns what the Phaeacians undertake; the exact sense is not certain. καὶ ἡμῖν 'to us also'; διαμπερές 'without a break'; ἐξ ἔτι πατρῶν 'from our fathers' time on', with an old genitive plural πατρῶν.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ πυγμάχοι εἰμὲν ἀμύμονες οὐδὲ παλαισταί,
ἀλλὰ ποσὶ κραιπνῶς θέομεν καὶ νηυσὶν ἄριστοι,
αἰεὶ δ’ ἡμῖν δαίς τε φίλη κίθαρίς τε χοροί τε
εἵματά τ’ ἐξημοιβὰ λοετρά τε θερμὰ καὶ εὐναί.
sentences.tr:
ou gar pygmachoi eimen amymones oude palaistai,
alla posi kraipnōs theomen kai nēusin aristoi,
aiei d’ hēmin dais te philē kitharis te choroi te
heimata t’ exēmoiba loetra te therma kai eunai.
sentences.l:
For not boxers, blameless, are we, nor wrestlers,
but with feet at a rush we run, and in ships are best,
and always to us the feast is dear, and the lyre, and dances,
and changes of clothes, and warm baths, and couches.
sentences.i: For we are not blameless boxers or wrestlers, but we run at a rush on our feet and are best in ships, and the feast is always dear to us, and the lyre and the dances, and changes of clothes and warm baths and couches.
sentences.n: γάρ explains the ἡμετέρης ἀρετῆς just named: the Phaeacians' excellence lies elsewhere than in the rough sports. εἰμέν is ἐσμέν 'we are'; πυγμάχοι 'boxers', παλαισταί 'wrestlers'. ἀμύμονες is 'blameless' by convention; the real meaning of ἀμύμων is not known, and 'blameless' is kept even where it sits oddly, as here of boxers. ποσὶ … θέομεν 'we run with our feet' (θέομεν is the present of θέω 'run'); κραιπνῶς is 'at a rush'; ἄριστοι 'best', with νηυσίν 'in ships' in the dative of respect. αἰεί is ἀεί 'always'. What follows is a list of nominatives: δαίς 'feast' (φίλη 'dear' agrees with it), κίθαρις 'lyre' (not claimed to differ from φόρμιγξ, which is also 'lyre'), χοροί 'dances', εἵματα ἐξημοιβά 'changes of clothes' (ἐξήμοιβος 'changed, for changing'), λοετρά 'baths', εὐναί 'couches'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε, Φαιήκων βητάρμονες ὅσσοι ἄριστοι,
παίσατε, ὥς χ’ ὁ ξεῖνος ἐνίσπῃ οἷσι φίλοισιν
οἴκαδε νοστήσας, ὅσσον περιγιγνόμεθ’ ἄλλων
ναυτιλίῃ καὶ ποσσὶ καὶ ὀρχηστυῖ καὶ ἀοιδῇ.
sentences.tr:
all’ age, Phaiēkōn bētarmones hossoi aristoi,
paisate, hōs ch’ ho xeinos enispēi hoisi philoisin
oikade nostēsas, hosson perigignometh’ allōn
nautiliēi kai possi kai orchēstui kai aoidēi.
sentences.l:
But come, of the Phaeacians the dancers, as many as are best,
play, so that the stranger may tell his own dear ones
when he has returned home, how much we surpass others
in seafaring and with feet and in dancing and song.
sentences.i: But come now, all you dancers of the Phaeacians who are best, play, so that the stranger may tell his own dear ones, when he has returned home, how far we surpass others in seafaring and running and dancing and song.
sentences.n: βητάρμονες are 'dancers'. ὅσσοι ἄριστοι 'as many as are best' gives the best of the dancers among the Phaeacians. παίσατε is the aorist imperative of παίζω 'play, sport', here of dancing, as the following lines show. ὥς χ’ is ὥς κε 'so that … may', with ἐνίσπῃ, the aorist subjunctive of ἐννέπω 'tell'. οἷσι φίλοισιν 'to his own dear ones' (οἷσι is the possessive ὅς again, in the dative plural). νοστήσας 'having come home' (from νόστος 'homecoming'); ὅσσον περιγιγνόμεθ’ ἄλλων 'how far we surpass others' (περιγίγνομαι with the genitive 'be superior to'). ναυτιλίῃ 'in seafaring', ποσσί 'with the feet', ὀρχηστυῖ 'in dancing' (ὀρχηστύς), ἀοιδῇ 'in song'.

sentences.t:
Δημοδόκῳ δέ τις αἶψα κιὼν φόρμιγγα λίγειαν
οἰσέτω, ἥ που κεῖται ἐν ἡμετέροισι δόμοισιν.
sentences.tr:
Dēmodokōi de tis aipsa kiōn phorminga ligeian
oisetō, hē pou keitai en hēmeteroisi domoisin.
sentences.l:
And to Demodocus let someone, going at once, the clear-sounding lyre
bring, which somewhere lies in our house.”
sentences.i: And let someone go at once and bring the clear-sounding lyre to Demodocus; it lies somewhere in our house.”
sentences.n: Δημοδόκῳ 'to Demodocus' is the dative of the person for whom the lyre is fetched; he is the singer. δέ τις 'and let some one'; κιών is the participle of κίω 'go', 'going'; οἰσέτω is the third-person imperative of φέρω, built on the future stem (οἴσω), 'let him carry'. λίγειαν 'clear-sounding' agrees with φόρμιγγα 'lyre'. ἥ που κεῖται 'which somewhere lies': ἥ is the relative, not the article, and που is 'somewhere, I suppose'. ἐν ἡμετέροισι δόμοισιν 'in our house', with the plural of δόμος for a single dwelling and the dative ending -οισι. The closing quotation mark ends Alcinous's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’ Ἀλκίνοος θεοείκελος, ὦρτο δὲ κῆρυξ
οἴσων φόρμιγγα γλαφυρὴν δόμου ἐκ βασιλῆος.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’ Alkinoos theoeikelos, ōrto de kēryx
oisōn phorminga glaphyrēn domou ek basilēos.
sentences.l:
So spoke Alcinous, god-resembling, and rose the herald
to carry the hollow lyre out of the house of the king.
sentences.i: So spoke Alcinous, who was like a god, and a herald set out to bring the hollow lyre from the king's house.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ 'so spoke' is ἔφατο, elided, followed by the name as at the end of any speech. θεοείκελος 'god-resembling' (from θεός 'god' and εἴκελος 'like') is a standing epithet. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι 'rouse', 'started up, set out', and κῆρυξ is 'herald'. οἴσων is the future participle of φέρω, 'to carry', expressing purpose. γλαφυρήν 'hollow' is the same word as in 'hollow caves', here of the lyre's body. δόμου ἐκ βασιλῆος 'out of the house of the king', with the Homeric genitive βασιλῆος of βασιλεύς.

sentences.t:
αἰσυμνῆται δὲ κριτοὶ ἐννέα πάντες ἀνέσταν
δήμιοι, οἳ κατ’ ἀγῶνας ἐὺ πρήσσεσκον ἕκαστα,
λείηναν δὲ χορόν, καλὸν δ’ εὔρυναν ἀγῶνα.
sentences.tr:
aisymnētai de kritoi ennea pantes anestan
dēmioi, hoi kat’ agōnas ey prēsseskon hekasta,
leiēnan de choron, kalon d’ eurynan agōna.
sentences.l:
and stewards, chosen, nine in all, stood up,
of the people, who at the gatherings used to manage each thing well,
and they smoothed the dancing-ground, and widened the fair gathering-place.
sentences.i: Nine stewards, chosen from the people, all stood up, men who used to manage every detail well at the gatherings, and they smoothed the dancing-ground and widened the fine gathering-place.
sentences.n: αἰσυμνῆται are men who preside over and arrange (presiding officers), here 'stewards' of the games, though how the word is formed is obscure; κριτοί 'chosen' is the verbal adjective of κρίνω 'pick out', and δήμιοι 'of the people, public'. ἐννέα πάντες 'nine, all of them'. ἀνέσταν is ἀνέστησαν, the aorist of ἀνίστημι in its intransitive sense 'stood up'. οἳ … ἐὺ πρήσσεσκον ἕκαστα: the ending -σκον makes the imperfect iterative, 'used to manage each thing well' (ἐύ 'well', ἕκαστα 'each detail'). λείηναν 'smoothed' (aorist of λειαίνω), εὔρυναν 'widened' (εὐρύνω). χορός is the dancing-ground here, though the word also means 'dance', and ἀγών is the ground where the people gather, 'gathering-place', as in ἐν ἀγῶνι above.

sentences.t:
κῆρυξ δ’ ἐγγύθεν ἦλθε φέρων φόρμιγγα λίγειαν
Δημοδόκῳ·
sentences.tr:
kēryx d’ engythen ēlthe pherōn phorminga ligeian
Dēmodokōi·
sentences.l:
And the herald came from close by, bringing the clear-sounding lyre
for Demodocus;
sentences.i: The herald came from close by, carrying the clear-sounding lyre to Demodocus;
sentences.n: ἐγγύθεν 'from close by' has the suffix -θεν, 'from'. φέρων 'carrying' takes φόρμιγγα λίγειαν 'the clear-sounding lyre', the same words as at 254, and Δημοδόκῳ is the dative 'for Demodocus'. The stop · after Δημοδόκῳ falls in the middle of line 262.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἔπειτα κί’ ἐς μέσον·
sentences.tr: ho d’ epeita ki’ es meson·
sentences.l: and he then went into the middle;
sentences.i: and he then went into the middle;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ 'and he' is the article as a pronoun, Demodocus. κί’ is κίε, the elided imperfect of κίω 'go'; ἐς μέσον 'into the middle', the middle of the ground that has been cleared. The stop · after μέσον falls in the middle of line 262.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ κοῦροι
πρωθῆβαι ἵσταντο, δαήμονες ὀρχηθμοῖο,
πέπληγον δὲ χορὸν θεῖον ποσίν.
sentences.tr:
amphi de kouroi
prōthēbai histanto, daēmones orchēthmoio,
peplēgon de choron theion posin.
sentences.l:
and around, youths
in the first of youth stood, skilled in dancing,
and struck the divine dancing-ground with their feet.
sentences.i: and round about stood youths in their first bloom, skilled in the dance, and they struck the divine dancing-ground with their feet.
sentences.n: ἀμφί is an adverb here, 'round about'. κοῦροι πρωθῆβαι 'youths in their first youth' (πρωθήβης, from πρῶτος and ἥβη 'youth'); ἵσταντο is the imperfect middle of ἵστημι, 'stood'. δαήμονες 'skilled' takes the genitive ὀρχηθμοῖο 'in dance', the -οιο ending being Attic -ου. πέπληγον is the aorist of πλήσσω 'strike', with epic reduplication and no augment; χορὸν θεῖον is 'the divine dancing-ground' (θεῖος 'divine'), and χορός is again the place, since it is what their feet strike. The stop after ποσίν falls in the middle of line 264.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
μαρμαρυγὰς θηεῖτο ποδῶν, θαύμαζε δὲ θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
autar Odysseus
marmarygas thēeito podōn, thaumaze de thymōi.
sentences.l:
But Odysseus
the flashings of their feet gazed at, and marvelled in his heart.
sentences.i: And Odysseus gazed at the flashing of their feet and marvelled in his heart.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ 'but, and' turns to Odysseus. μαρμαρυγάς 'flashings, twinklings' (from μαρμαίρω 'flash') is the object of θηεῖτο, the imperfect of θηέομαι 'gaze at in wonder', and ποδῶν 'of their feet' is the genitive that goes with μαρμαρυγάς. θαύμαζε 'marvelled' is the unaugmented imperfect of θαυμάζω; θυμῷ 'in his heart' (θυμός).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ φορμίζων ἀνεβάλλετο καλὸν ἀείδειν
ἀμφ’ Ἄρεος φιλότητος εὐστεφάνου τ’ Ἀφροδίτης,
sentences.tr:
autar ho phormizōn aneballeto kalon aeidein
amph’ Areos philotētos eustephanou t’ Aphroditēs,
sentences.l:
But he, playing the lyre, struck up to sing finely
of the love of Ares and of fair-crowned Aphrodite,
sentences.i: But he, playing his lyre, began to sing beautifully of the love of Ares and of fair-crowned Aphrodite,
sentences.n: ὁ φορμίζων is 'he, playing the lyre' (φορμίζω, from φόρμιγξ), the article ὁ being 'he', Demodocus. ἀνεβάλλετο is the imperfect middle of ἀναβάλλομαι 'strike up, begin (a song)', with the infinitive ἀείδειν 'to sing', and καλόν, the neuter as an adverb, 'finely, beautifully'. ἀμφ’ 'about' governs φιλότητος 'love' (the word also names the act of love) and the two genitives Ἄρεος and Ἀφροδίτης 'of Ares … of Aphrodite'. εὐστεφάνου 'fair-crowned' (ἐύ- 'fair' and στέφανος 'crown') is a standing epithet. The sentence is long, so it is cut at the comma.

sentences.t:
ὡς τὰ πρῶτα μίγησαν ἐν Ἡφαίστοιο δόμοισι
λάθρῃ, πολλὰ δ’ ἔδωκε, λέχος δ’ ᾔσχυνε καὶ εὐνὴν
Ἡφαίστοιο ἄνακτος.
sentences.tr:
hōs ta prōta migēsan en Hēphaistoio domoisi
lathrēi, polla d’ edōke, lechos d’ ēischyne kai eunēn
Hēphaistoio anaktos.
sentences.l:
how first they were joined in the house of Hephaestus
in secret, and many things he gave, and the bed he dishonoured, and the couch
of lord Hephaestus.
sentences.i: how they first lay together in the house of Hephaestus, in secret, and how he gave many gifts and dishonoured the bed and couch of lord Hephaestus.
sentences.n: ὡς here is 'how', introducing what the song tells of (an indirect statement after ἀείδειν). τὰ πρῶτα 'at first' is an adverbial accusative; μίγησαν 'they were joined, they lay together' is the aorist passive of μίγνυμι; Ἡφαίστοιο δόμοισι 'in the house of Hephaestus', with the genitive in -οιο; λάθρῃ 'in secret'. The subject changes: πολλὰ δ’ ἔδωκε, λέχος δ’ ᾔσχυνε 'and he gave many things, and disgraced the bed', where 'he' is Ares; the Greek does not say who received the gifts. ᾔσχυνε is the aorist of αἰσχύνω 'disgrace'; λέχος 'bed' and εὐνήν 'couch' are two words for the marriage bed. Ἡφαίστοιο ἄνακτος 'of lord Hephaestus'. The stop after ἄνακτος falls in the middle of line 270.

sentences.t:
ἄφαρ δέ οἱ ἄγγελος ἦλθεν
Ἥλιος, ὅ σφ’ ἐνόησε μιγαζομένους φιλότητι.
sentences.tr:
aphar de hoi angelos ēlthen
Hēlios, ho sph’ enoēse migazomenous philotēti.
sentences.l:
And at once to him a messenger came
the Sun, who noticed them mingling in love.
sentences.i: At once the Sun, who had noticed them lying together in love, came to him as a messenger.
sentences.n: ἄφαρ 'at once'. οἱ is 'to him', Hephaestus; ἄγγελος 'as a messenger' stands in apposition to Ἥλιος 'the Sun', the god himself. ὅ σφ’ ἐνόησε: ὅ is here the relative (Attic ὅς), 'who', σφ’ is σφε 'them', and ἐνόησε is the aorist of νοέω 'notice, perceive'. μιγαζομένους 'mingling' (μιγάζομαι, a lengthened form of μίγνυμι) with φιλότητι 'in love'.

sentences.t:
Ἥφαιστος δ’ ὡς οὖν θυμαλγέα μῦθον ἄκουσε,
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ἐς χαλκεῶνα κακὰ φρεσὶ βυσσοδομεύων,
ἐν δ’ ἔθετ’ ἀκμοθέτῳ μέγαν ἄκμονα, κόπτε δὲ δεσμοὺς
ἀρρήκτους ἀλύτους, ὄφρ’ ἔμπεδον αὖθι μένοιεν.
sentences.tr:
Hēphaistos d’ hōs oun thymalgea mython akouse,
bē rh’ imen es chalkeōna kaka phresi byssodomeuōn,
en d’ ethet’ akmothetōi megan akmona, kopte de desmous
arrēktous alytous, ophr’ empedon authi menoien.
sentences.l:
And Hephaestus, when then the heart-paining word he heard,
set out to go to the smithy, evil in his wits deep-devising,
and set on the anvil-block a great anvil, and hammered bonds
unbreakable, not to be undone, so that firmly on the spot they would stay.
sentences.i: And when Hephaestus heard the word that pained his heart, he set out for the smithy, devising evil deep in his mind, and set a great anvil on its block, and hammered out bonds that could not be broken or undone, so that they would stay fast right there.
sentences.n: ὡς … ἄκουσε 'when he heard' (ὡς unaccented is 'when' here; ἄκουσε is the aorist of ἀκούω, without augment). θυμαλγέα 'heart-paining' (θυμός 'heart' and ἄλγος 'pain') agrees with μῦθον 'word, report'. βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν is a stock phrase, 'he set out to go' (βῆ is ἔβη without the augment). ἐς χαλκεῶνα 'to the smithy'. κακὰ φρεσὶ βυσσοδομεύων 'devising evil in his mind, deep down': βυσσοδομεύω is 'build in the depths', of a plot kept hidden, and φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν. ἐν … ἔθετο is tmesis 'set on', with ἀκμοθέτῳ 'anvil-block' and ἄκμονα 'anvil'. κόπτε 'was hammering' takes δεσμούς 'bonds', described by the two adjectives ἀρρήκτους ἀλύτους 'unbreakable, not to be undone'. ὄφρ’ … μένοιεν is 'so that they might stay', the optative of purpose after a past tense; ἔμπεδον 'firm, fast'; αὖθι 'on the spot'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ τεῦξε δόλον κεχολωμένος Ἄρει,
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ἐς θάλαμον, ὅθι οἱ φίλα δέμνι’ ἔκειτο,
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἑρμῖσιν χέε δέσματα κύκλῳ ἁπάντῃ·
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē teuxe dolon kecholōmenos Arei,
bē rh’ imen es thalamon, hothi hoi phila demni’ ekeito,
amphi d’ ar’ hermisin chee desmata kyklōi hapantēi·
sentences.i: And when, angry with Ares, he had fashioned the trick, he set out for the bedchamber where his own dear bed lay, and poured the bonds round the bedposts in a circle all about;
sentences.n: τεῦξε is the aorist of τεύχω 'make, fashion', without the augment. δόλον 'trick' is both the trick and the device that carries it out; here it is the net of bonds. κεχολωμένος is the perfect participle of χολόομαι 'be angry', with the dative Ἄρει 'with Ares'. θάλαμον 'chamber'; ὅθι 'where'; οἱ … φίλα δέμνια 'his own dear bed', with οἱ the dative of possession 'for him' and δέμνια the neuter plural for a single bed; ἔκειτο 'lay' takes a singular verb with a neuter plural. ἀμφί … χέε 'poured round' is tmesis; ἑρμῖσιν 'bedposts' (dative plural of ἕρμις); δέσματα 'bonds'; κύκλῳ ἁπάντῃ 'in a circle all round'.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ καὶ καθύπερθε μελαθρόφιν ἐξεκέχυντο,
ἠύτ’ ἀράχνια λεπτά, τά γ’ οὔ κέ τις οὐδὲ ἴδοιτο,
οὐδὲ θεῶν μακάρων·
sentences.tr:
polla de kai kathyperthe melathrophin exekechynto,
ēyt’ arachnia lepta, ta g’ ou ke tis oude idoito,
oude theōn makarōn·
sentences.i: and many more hung down from above, from the roof-beam, like fine spider-webs, which no one could see, not even any of the blessed gods;
sentences.n: πολλά 'many' is the neuter plural for the many bonds. καθύπερθε 'from above'; μελαθρόφιν 'from the roof-beam', where -φιν is an old ending of place and source and μέλαθρον is the roof-beam; ἐξεκέχυντο is the pluperfect passive of ἐκχέω 'pour out', 'had streamed down, hung down'. ἠύτ’ is ἠύτε 'like'; ἀράχνια λεπτά 'fine spider-webs'. τά γ’ οὔ κέ τις οὐδὲ ἴδοιτο: τά is the relative 'which', and κε with the optative ἴδοιτο (aorist of ὁράω) is 'would see'. οὐδὲ … 'not even' brings in θεῶν μακάρων 'of the blessed gods'. The stop · after μακάρων falls in the middle of line 281.

sentences.t: πέρι γὰρ δολόεντα τέτυκτο.
sentences.tr: peri gar doloenta tetykto.
sentences.l: for exceedingly guileful they had been made.
sentences.i: for they had been made exceedingly guileful.
sentences.n: πέρι is an adverb here, 'exceedingly', and γάρ 'for' gives the reason why no one, not even a god, could see them. δολόεντα 'guileful, full of trickery' is from δόλος, the word for the trick at 276, and agrees with the bonds; τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω, the verb of τεῦξε at 276.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ πάντα δόλον περὶ δέμνια χεῦεν,
εἴσατ’ ἴμεν ἐς Λῆμνον, ἐυκτίμενον πτολίεθρον,
ἥ οἱ γαιάων πολὺ φιλτάτη ἐστὶν ἁπασέων.
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē panta dolon peri demnia cheuen,
eisat’ imen es Lēmnon, eyktimenon ptoliethron,
hē hoi gaiaōn poly philtatē estin hapaseōn.
sentences.l:
But when he had poured the whole trick about the bed,
he started off to go to Lemnos, the well-built citadel,
which to him of all lands by far is dearest.
sentences.i: And when he had spread the whole trick around the bed, he started off for Lemnos, the well-built citadel, which is by far the dearest to him of all lands.
sentences.n: πάντα δόλον 'the whole trick'; περὶ δέμνια 'around the bed'; χεῦεν is the aorist of χέω 'pour', with the epic ending (Attic ἔχεεν). εἴσατ’ is εἴσατο, an aorist whose origin is disputed: it is usually taken as 'started off' (from ἵημι), though some read 'seemed, made as if to go'; ἴμεν is the infinitive ἰέναι, so 'started off to go'. Λῆμνον, ἐυκτίμενον πτολίεθρον 'Lemnos, the well-built citadel'. ἥ οἱ … ἐστίν 'which to him is', where ἥ is the relative and οἱ is 'to him'. γαιάων is the epic genitive plural of γαῖα 'land', φιλτάτη 'dearest' the superlative of φίλος, and ἁπασέων is Attic ἁπασῶν 'of all'.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἀλαοσκοπιὴν εἶχε χρυσήνιος Ἄρης,
ὡς ἴδεν Ἥφαιστον κλυτοτέχνην νόσφι κιόντα·
sentences.tr:
oud’ alaoskopiēn eiche chrysēnios Arēs,
hōs iden Hēphaiston klytotechnēn nosphi kionta·
sentences.l:
and no blind man's watch kept golden-reined Ares,
when he saw Hephaestus, famous in craft, going away;
sentences.i: And golden-reined Ares kept no blind man's watch when he saw Hephaestus, famous in craft, going off;
sentences.n: ἀλαοσκοπιήν is built from ἀλαός 'blind', the word Athena used at 195, and σκοπιή 'lookout', so 'a blind man's watch', a careless lookout. εἶχε 'kept' is the imperfect of ἔχω. χρυσήνιος 'golden-reined' (χρυσός 'gold', ἡνία 'reins') is a standing epithet of Ares. ὡς ἴδεν 'when he saw' (ἴδεν is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω). κλυτοτέχνην 'famous in craft' (κλυτός 'famous', τέχνη 'craft') is an epithet of Hephaestus; νόσφι κιόντα 'going away' (νόσφι 'apart, away', κιόντα the participle of κίω 'go').

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι πρὸς δῶμα περικλυτοῦ Ἡφαίστοιο
ἰσχανόων φιλότητος ἐυστεφάνου Κυθερείης.
sentences.tr:
bē d’ ienai pros dōma periklytou Hēphaistoio
ischanoōn philotētos eystephanou Kythereiēs.
sentences.l:
and set out to go to the house of very-famous Hephaestus,
longing for the love of fair-crowned Cytherea.
sentences.i: and set out for the house of the very famous Hephaestus, longing for the love of fair-crowned Cytherea.
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι 'and he set out to go' is the βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν pattern again, with ἰέναι for ἴμεν; πρὸς δῶμα 'to the house'. περικλυτοῦ 'very famous' (περί here 'exceedingly', κλυτός 'famous'); Ἡφαίστοιο is the genitive in -οιο. ἰσχανόων is the participle of ἰσχανάω, 'hold oneself back, be eager', taken with the genitive φιλότητος 'love' as 'longing for'. ἐυστεφάνου 'fair-crowned'; Κυθερείης 'of Cytherea' is a name of Aphrodite that comes from the island of Cythera.

sentences.t:
ἡ δὲ νέον παρὰ πατρὸς ἐρισθενέος Κρονίωνος
ἐρχομένη κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζεθ’·
sentences.tr:
hē de neon para patros eristheneos Kroniōnos
erchomenē kat’ ar’ hezeth’·
sentences.l:
And she, only now from her father, of great strength, the son of Cronus,
coming, sat down;
sentences.i: She had just come from her father, the son of Cronus, great in strength, and sat down;
sentences.n: ἡ δέ 'and she' is the article as a pronoun, Aphrodite. νέον is an adverb, 'just now, newly'; παρὰ πατρός 'from her father'. ἐρισθενέος 'of great strength' (ἐρι- 'very', σθένος 'strength') and Κρονίωνος 'son of Cronus' are two epithets in place of a name, Κρονίων being a way of naming Zeus, so that her father is not named. ἐρχομένη 'coming'. κατὰ … ἕζεθ’ is tmesis, 'sat down'; ἕζεθ’ is ἕζετο, the unaugmented imperfect of ἕζομαι 'sit'. The stop · after ἕζεθ’ falls in the middle of line 290.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ εἴσω δώματος ᾔει,
ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρί, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ eisō dōmatos ēiei,
en t’ ara hoi phy cheiri, epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l:
and he was going inside the house,
and clasped her by the hand, and spoke a word, and called her by name:
sentences.i: and he came into the house, took her hand, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ 'and he' is Ares. εἴσω δώματος 'inside the house' (εἴσω with the genitive), and ᾔει is the imperfect of εἶμι 'go', 'was going'. The last line is a stock formula for coming up to someone and addressing them: ἔν … φῦ is tmesis, 'grew fast to', from the aorist of φύω without the augment, with οἱ 'to her' and χειρί 'by the hand', so 'took firm hold of her by the hand'; ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε is 'spoke a word and called her by name', with ἔφατ’ for ἔφατο and ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε in tmesis. His words are not in this part, so no quotation mark is opened.
